opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important empirical questions for thinking about how fast things go once AIs can automate AI research. There are a few angles I'd take.

The most direct one is to look at what's happening inside AI companies right now. You could ask researchers how they'd spend their time if they had twice as much compute, or half as much. How much of their day is waiting on experiments versus thinking, writing code, or reading results? If people say "honestly, I'd just run the same experiments a bit faster," that suggests compute isn't the main bottleneck. If they say "I have a backlog of twenty ideas and I can only test two," that points the other way. Surveys like that are noisy, but they're cheap and informative.

A second angle is natural variation. Different labs, and different teams within labs, have very different amounts of compute per researcher. Academic groups have far less than frontier labs. You can ask how much their research productivity differs. It's hard to control for talent and selection, but you can still learn something, especially about whether smaller-compute groups find clever ways to substitute labor for compute, like doing more careful small-scale experiments that extrapolate.

Third, you can look at the history of algorithmic progress. People have estimated how much efficiency has improved over time on things like image classification or language modeling. You can ask how much of that came from ideas that required large-scale experiments to discover versus ideas you could have found at small scale. Many important advances, like architectural tweaks or better optimizers, can be validated reasonably well at small scale. But some things, like emergent capabilities or scaling-law behavior, really do need big runs.

The framing I find most useful is an economic one: think of research output as a production function of cognitive labor and compute, and ask about the elasticity of substitution between them. If they're strong complements, then even if you get millions of AI researchers, progress is capped by experiment throughput. If they're fairly substitutable, extra smart labor can squeeze much more out of fixed compute: designing better experiments, running smaller proxies, being more careful about which ideas to test, writing more efficient code. My guess is the substitutability is higher than a lot of people assume, because currently human researchers are pretty sloppy with compute, since human time is the scarce thing. If labor became abundant, you'd optimize really hard on compute efficiency.

Finally, you could run more controlled experiments. Give teams, or AI agents, fixed research tasks with different compute budgets and see how performance scales. As AI agents get better at research, this becomes much more feasible, because you can vary compute and labor independently in ways you can't with humans.

None of these is decisive alone, but together they'd give a much better sense of whether an intelligence explosion would be heavily throttled by compute or could proceed pretty fast on software improvements alone.

r001.rationale: The response proposes comparing teams with different compute levels, but does not describe accidental or exogenous changes in allocations.

r002.rationale: It says abundant AI research labor could change compute use: researchers might optimize harder for compute efficiency when human time is no longer scarce.

r003.rationale: It notes confounding in comparisons across labs, but does not state that natural experiments reveal only local returns to compute.

r004.rationale: It proposes varying compute for teams or AI agents on fixed tasks, but does not specify human teams, budgets resembling those anticipated for AI researchers, or measuring research speed.

r005.rationale: It suggests researchers could optimize compute use, but does not describe an initial slowdown under tighter constraints that diminishes as they adapt.

r006.rationale: It does not say that AI researchers would operate faster and therefore have substantial opportunity to learn to work within compute constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a question I think about a lot, because it bears pretty directly on what happens once you have AIs that can do AI research — like, if you've got automated researchers, how much does that actually speed things up, versus you just hit a wall because you're bottlenecked on compute for experiments.

So I think there are a few different angles I'd want to take.

The first one is just: go ask the people doing the work. Like, talk to researchers at frontier labs and ask them, "If you had ten times the compute, how much faster would your research go?" Or the inverse: "If you had a tenth of the compute, how much would it slow you down?" And I think you'd get pretty varied answers, but my sense is that a lot of people would say something like, "Yeah, more compute would help a lot, but it's not the only thing — I'm also bottlenecked on my own time, on having good ideas, on engineering effort to actually run the experiments." And the interesting thing is that if you're in a world where you've automated the labor side, those other bottlenecks go away, and then the compute bottleneck becomes relatively more binding.

The second angle is kind of a natural experiment approach. You can look at historical cases where compute per researcher varied a lot. So, for example, you could compare labs that had very different amounts of compute per researcher and see how that affected their output. Or you could look within a lab over time — like, labs have scaled up compute massively over the last several years, and you could ask how much of the research progress tracks that versus tracks headcount or something. The problem is that this is pretty confounded, because the labs with more compute also tend to have better researchers and better infrastructure, and they're also often spending the compute on bigger training runs rather than on more experiments per researcher. So you'd have to be careful about that.

A third angle — which I actually think is maybe the most informative — is to think about what the marginal experiment looks like. So, what fraction of the compute at a lab is going into the big flagship training runs versus into the smaller-scale experiments that actually drive algorithmic progress? And my understanding is that a lot of the algorithmic progress actually comes from relatively small-scale experiments, where you're running at, say, a thousandth or a ten-thousandth of frontier scale, and then you're scaling up the things that work. If that's true, then compute for experiments is actually a smaller fraction of the overall compute budget than you might think, and the question becomes: how well do those small-scale results transfer? And how much would you gain from running way more of them?

And then I think the fourth thing is you can just try to directly estimate it with a kind of model. Like, you say: suppose we have a million automated researchers, each running at, I don't know, ten times human speed. How much compute would they want to use for experiments? And then you compare that to how much compute is actually available. And I think when you do that calculation, you find that — at least naively — they'd want far more compute than is available, which suggests compute would be a serious bottleneck. But the catch is that automated researchers might also just be much better at being compute-efficient. They could do more careful experimental design, they could run things at smaller scale, they could think harder before running experiments. So there's a kind of substitution between labor and compute, and the question is how elastic that substitution is.

I guess the honest answer is that I don't think any one of these methods gives you a clean answer. But I think if you combined them — talked to researchers, looked at the historical data, thought carefully about where the marginal compute is actually going — you'd get a reasonable picture. And my current best guess is that compute is a meaningful bottleneck but not a total one. Like, I'd guess that if you had unlimited automated labor but the same compute, you'd still get maybe a several-x speedup in algorithmic progress, rather than it being either totally unconstrained or basically no speedup at all. But I hold that pretty loosely.

r001.rationale: It proposes comparing labs with different compute levels and tracking changes over time, but does not describe accidental or exogenous changes in compute allocation.

r002.rationale: It says automating research labor removes other bottlenecks, making compute relatively more binding than it is for human researchers.

r003.rationale: It notes confounding in historical comparisons but does not say those comparisons reveal only local returns to compute.

r004.rationale: It suggests asking researchers about hypothetical compute levels and comparing historical labs, but not assigning teams different budgets, including AI-researcher-like budgets, to measure research speed.

r005.rationale: It mentions that automated researchers could use compute more efficiently, but does not suggest an initial slowdown under tighter constraints would diminish as researchers adapt.

r006.rationale: It posits automated researchers operating faster than humans and potentially using compute more efficiently, but does not say their faster operation gives them substantial opportunity to learn to work within constraints.

astra-6.text:
I’d try to separate two questions. One is how much faster you make progress if you have more compute. The other is how much useful research you can do while using relatively little compute. Those aren’t quite the same, because researchers can change what they work on depending on the resources available.

An experiment I’d be interested in is giving comparable research teams substantially different compute budgets and seeing what happens. Ideally, you’d have enough teams that differences in researcher ability and choice of project don’t dominate the result. You’d want to measure actual improvements on some shared objective, rather than just how many experiments they run or papers they produce.

You could also look at individual research projects and ask: Where did the time go? Were people waiting for experiments to finish? Did they have promising experiments they couldn’t afford to run? Or was the bottleneck coming up with an idea, implementing it correctly, or understanding the results? More compute helps with some of those things much more directly than others.

The tricky part is that the answer might change a lot when you have AI systems doing the research. If thinking and writing code become much cheaper, then experiments could become the dominant cost. But the systems might also get better at choosing informative experiments or doing research at a smaller scale. So I’d particularly want to measure how research output changes as you vary both the amount of researcher effort and the experimental compute budget, rather than treating compute as a single, fixed bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response proposes deliberately giving teams different compute budgets, not using accidental or exogenous allocation changes.

r002.rationale: It says the answer could change when AI systems do research because thinking and coding become cheaper, shifting experiments’ role as a cost and potentially changing how compute is used.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss natural experiments or say they reveal only local returns to compute.

r004.rationale: It compares teams with different compute budgets and measures progress, but does not specify human teams, budgets resembling those anticipated for AI researchers, or research speed.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that an initial slowdown under tighter constraints might diminish as researchers adapt.

r006.rationale: It does not say faster AI researchers would have substantial opportunity to learn to work within compute constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d try to separate a few different questions. One is: if you gave a research team ten times as much compute, how much faster would they make progress? Another is: if you held their compute fixed, how much could they improve their results just by finding better ways to use it? Those are related, but they’re not the same question.

Ideally, you’d run an experiment where you gave otherwise similar teams different compute budgets and measured what they accomplished. That’s pretty expensive, and measuring research progress is difficult. You don’t want to just measure how many experiments they run, because the value of experiments varies enormously.

A more practical starting point would be to look closely at particular research projects. What experiments did people want to run but couldn’t? How long were they waiting for results? And, if they’d had substantially more compute, would they actually have known what to do with it? You could make those predictions in advance and then give some projects additional compute to see whether the predictions hold up.

I’d also be interested in whether the constraint changes as you automate more of the research. If you make it much cheaper to generate ideas and implement experiments, then compute could become a much bigger bottleneck, even if it wasn’t the main bottleneck for human researchers. So I’d be wary of taking an estimate from the current research process and assuming it applies to a substantially different one.

r001.rationale: The response proposes assigning different compute budgets in an experiment, but does not propose using accidental or exogenous allocation changes.

r002.rationale: It says automating idea generation and experiments could make compute a much bigger bottleneck than it is for human researchers, indicating that returns may differ with AI research.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss natural experiments or state that they reveal only local returns to compute.

r004.rationale: It proposes comparing similar teams with different compute budgets and measuring progress, but does not specify budgets resembling those anticipated for AI researchers.

r005.rationale: It mentions improving how compute is used, but does not say an initial slowdown from tighter constraints may diminish as researchers adapt.

r006.rationale: It does not state that faster AI researchers would have substantial opportunity to learn to work within compute constraints.
